Rossie D. Alston Jr.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR TARGETED
VACATUR OF ECF NOS. 64 AND 84, WITHDRAWAL OR MODIFICATION OF THE
MAGISTRATE-JUDGE REFERRAL, AND RELATED INTERIM RELIEF

I. THE REQUESTED CORRECTION

Two signed financial disclosure reports of Magistrate Judge Davis list “FB common stock”
at year-end 2024 and year-end 2025, each with a value of $15,001 to $50,000. Ex. A at 2; Ex. B at
4. FB common stock is the common stock of Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. Two orders entered
during the Magistrate Judge’s participation in this action carry continuing procedural effects. ECF
No. 64 conditioned consideration of the proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint
on a comparison document due within two days. ECF No. 84 denied the amendment motion for
nonproduction of that document and denied two discovery motions, one directed to Meta, on the

stated ground that discovery had not begun.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 14 PagelD# 958

This Motion asks the District Judge to remove those continuing effects and to adjudicate
the affected motions on the submissions already of record. Two questions are presented, and they
are different. Whether participation violated 28 U.S.C. § 455 is the statutory question. Whether the
affected orders should be vacated is the remedial question. The disqualification motion before the
Magistrate Judge presents the first. This Motion presents the second, together with the referral and
interim questions that only the District Judge can decide. The merits of the underlying claims are
not argued here. They are argued in the Rule 72(a) objections and the amendment briefing, which
this Motion preserves.

II. AUTHORITY AND PROCEDURAL POSTURE
A. Referral and district-judge review.

A district judge may designate a magistrate judge to determine pretrial matters, and may
“reconsider any pretrial matter under this subparagraph (A) where it has been shown that the
magistrate judge’s order is clearly erroneous or contrary to law.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Rule
72(a) implements that review on timely objection. The referral itself remains within the District
Judge’s control; the statute designates and the District Judge may withdraw or modify the
designation. Plaintiff does not invoke 28 U.S.C. § 636(c)(4), which governs consensual civil-trial
referrals, and does not contend that its standard applies to this ordinary pretrial referral. The Fourth
Circuit treats a ruling that “relies on erroneous factual or legal premises” as an abuse of discretion
correctable on Rule 72(a) review. Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214, 217, 220 (4th Cir. 2022).

B. Interlocutory revision under Rule 54(b).

An order “that adjudicates fewer than all the claims . . . may be revised at any time before
the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). The Fourth Circuit reads
that text to give “broader flexibility to revise interlocutory orders before final judgment as the

litigation develops and new facts or arguments come to light,” and permits revision where there is

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 14 PagelD# 959

“substantially different evidence,” a change in applicable law, or clear error causing “manifest
injustice.” Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). That discretion “is not
limitless,” and a party may not use Rule 54(b) to repeat evidence or arguments the court has already
considered. Id. at 325-26. Plaintiff invokes Rule 54(b) as additional authority for the District
Judge’s revision of ECF Nos. 64 and 84. Plaintiff does not invoke it to revive any reconsideration
request to the Magistrate Judge, and does not contend that it extends any Rule 72(a) deadline. The
financial disclosure reports are evidence that no court in this action has considered. They are not a
repetition of anything previously presented.

C. The retrospective remedy.

Section 455 “neither prescribes nor prohibits any particular remedy for a violation of that
duty.” Liljeberg v. Health Servs. Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 862 (1988). The remedial
inquiry considers “the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that the denial of
relief will produce injustice in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public’s confidence in
the judicial process.” Id. at 864. Liljeberg applied that inquiry to a final judgment under Rule 60(b)
(6). The orders targeted here are interlocutory. Plaintiff does not invoke Rule 60(b)(6). The three
considerations govern the remedial question whatever the procedural vehicle, and the District
Judge’s authority over interlocutory orders under § 636(b)(1)(A) and Rule 54(b) supplies the
vehicle.

ECF No. 64 is already before the District Judge on timely objections submitted September
13, 2026. ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68. Those objections challenge the informational premise, the baseline,
and the deadline. This Motion adds the financial-conflict evidence as a separate basis for relief
from ECF No. 64. It does not suggest that the period to object to ECF No. 64 has restarted, and it
does not depend on that period.

Tl. THE FINANCIAL PREDICATE AND THE PERIOD REQUIRING REVIEW

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 14 PagelD# 960

The chronology is short. Judge Davis certified the 2024 report on August 18, 2025. Ex. B at
1, 8. He certified the 2025 report on May 14 and May 26, 2026. Ex. A at 1. Plaintiff filed this action,
naming Meta, on July 30, 2026. ECF No. 1. Meta appeared, moved to dismiss, and filed its
corporate disclosure statement on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24. Judge Davis entered ECF
No. 64 on September 9, 2026 and ECF No. 84 on October 7, 2026. Plaintiff was unaware of the
reported financial interest when ECF No. 84 was entered and promptly presented the issue after
learning of it. Ballentine Decl. { 2.

Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification where the judge “knows that he, individually or
as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household, has a financial interest in the
subject matter in controversy or in a party to the proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). A financial
interest is “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” Id. § 455(d)(4). “It is well-
established that the ownership of stock constitutes a ‘financial interest.’” Shell Oil Co. v. United
States, 672 F.3d 1283, 1289 (Fed. Cir. 2012); accord Cent. Tel. Co. of Va. v. Sprint Commc’ns Co.
of Va., Inc., 715 F.3d 501, 515 (4th Cir. 2013). Subsection (b)(4) requires knowledge. Liljeberg,
486 U.S. at 859. The fund exception in § 455(d)(4)(i) applies where shares are held through a
mutual or common investment fund managed without the judge’s input. Cent. Tel., 715 F.3d at 516.
The reports list the FB holding as common stock and list funds and an IRA as separate line items.
Ex. A at 2-3; Ex. B at 4-6. Whether the holding is in fact held through a qualifying arrangement is
a fact for determination.

Section 455(a) requires disqualification “in any proceeding in which his impartiality might
reasonably be questioned.” The inquiry is objective and does not require knowledge. Liljeberg, 486
U.S. at 859-60. Whether an objective observer would question impartiality depends on the

circumstances, including the judge’s knowledge before the action was filed, “what happened while

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 14 PagelD# 961

the case was pending before him, and what he did when he learned” of the interest. Id. at 856.
Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(a) applies without regard to those circumstances. Plaintiff
contends that those circumstances must be determined and that, on the facts the reports support, an
informed observer would question the impartiality of a judge deciding discovery directed to a
company whose stock the judge reported holding five months earlier.

Section 455(f) relieves a judge of disqualification where the interest is discovered after
assignment, substantial judicial time has been devoted to the matter, the interest could not be
substantially affected by the outcome, and the judge divests. 28 U.S.C. § 455(f). Each condition is
factual. Divestiture requires that the interest be “sold or given away”; placement in a blind trust
does not qualify. Centripetal Networks, Inc. v. Cisco Sys., Inc., 38 F.4th 1025 (Fed. Cir. 2022).
Whether divestiture cures earlier participation depends on how far the litigation had advanced and
what decisions were rendered in the interim. Litovich v. Bank of Am. Corp., 106 F.4th 218 (2d Cir.
2024). Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(f) is categorically unavailable. Plaintiff contends that
its conditions must be determined on the record, and that a present disposition of the interest, if one
has occurred or occurs, does not by itself resolve the effect of participation before it. The
retrospective determination requested here remains live whether or not present recusal becomes
unnecessary.

IV. THE THREE LILJEBERG CONSIDERATIONS SUPPORT VACATUR
A. Risk of injustice to the parties.

The concrete effect of the two orders is procedural. ECF No. 64 supplied a condition on
consideration of ECF No. 59. ECF No. 84 used nonproduction of the conditioned document to
exclude the proposed pleading from consideration and, separately, rejected the discovery requests
on the stated ground that discovery had not begun. The result is that three dismissal motions will be

decided against a pleading Plaintiff moved to replace, without seven closed answers about records

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 14 PagelD# 962

only Defendants hold. Plaintiff does not contend that losing a motion establishes injustice. The
injustice identified is adjudication of those motions by a judge who, on the evidence, held a
financial interest in the party whose discovery request he denied, with the consequence that the
completed submissions were never reached on their merits.

The proposed correction preserves completed briefing. Every submission on ECF Nos. 15,
54, and 59, including Defendants’ oppositions at ECF Nos. 33, 73, 74, and 83 and the reply
accepted by ECF No. 82, remains of record and is determined as it stands. No party begins again.
Defendants have an interest in retaining favorable rulings and in prompt resolution. Independent
determination on the existing submissions addresses that interest: it supplies a decision by a judge
whose participation is not questioned, on the same papers, without treating the challenged rulings
as controlling. The Federal Circuit, reviewing a judgment of this District, rejected the argument
that a judge’s prior rulings should stand because they were decided before he learned of his wife’s
interest, and rejected the argument that vacatur requires a showing of actual bias. Centripetal, 38
F.4th 1025. “Unlike § 455(a), [§ 455(b)(4)] is not triggered by an appearance of impropriety, but by
a known financial interest, which creates not only an appearance of impropriety but impropriety
itself.” Id.

B. Risk of injustice in other cases.

The second consideration asks whether denial of relief “will produce injustice in other
cases.” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. A remedy confined to prospective recusal leaves every order
entered during the disqualification in force. The statute’s duty to inform, § 455(c), and its bar on
waiver of subsection (b) grounds, § 455(e), assume that participation during a known financial
conflict has consequences beyond the judge’s future participation. Vacatur where the statutory and
remedial findings are made “may prevent a substantive injustice in some future case by

encouraging a judge or litigant to more carefully examine possible grounds for disqualification.”

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 94 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 14 PagelD# 963

Id. at 868. The remedy requested is not discipline. It addresses the legal effect of judicial
participation during an established disqualification, and it addresses nothing else.

C. Public confidence.

The third consideration is the objective concern created by adjudication involving a
corporate party in which a qualifying interest was held. The Federal Circuit ordered vacatur under
§ 455(b)(4) where “there [wa]s neither an allegation nor suggestion that the judge was unduly
influenced by his wife’s financial interest, which no one argues was substantial.” Shell Oil, 672
F.3d at 1291. The statute “simply requires recusal whenever financial conflicts of interest exist,
regardless of whether those conflicts affect the outcome of the case.” Id. Plaintiff makes no claim
of actual influence, no claim that this action is economically significant to Meta, and no claim of
improper intent. The concern is the one the statute identifies: a judge deciding whether a party may
be required to answer three questions about its own records, while reporting ownership of that
party’s stock.

Liljeberg leaves room for harmless error. 486 U.S. at 862. Not every violation requires
vacatur of every order, and the Federal Circuit has stated the rule the same way: “mandatory
recusal does not require mandatory vacatur.” Shell Oil, 672 F.3d at 1293. Plaintiff addresses
harmlessness in Part V rather than avoiding it.

V. THE FINANCIAL-CONFLICT VACATUR DECISIONS AND THE QUESTION
OF HARMLESSNESS

Three decisions apply the separate disqualification and remedy inquiries to financial
conflicts. Shell Oil held that a trial judge whose spouse held stock in the parent of two parties was
required to disqualify himself “from the entire proceeding,” that severing the affected parties did
not satisfy that requirement, and that vacatur was the appropriate remedy on the Liljeberg factors.

672 F.3d at 1290-93. Centripetal arose in this District. The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of a

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 14 PagelD# 964

recusal motion, vacated every order entered after the judge learned of his wife’s interest in a party,
and remanded for proceedings before a different judge, observing that “[a]llowing the same judge
to reaffirm his own rulings would severely undermine § 455.” 38 F.4th 1025. Litovich vacated a
judgment under § 455(a) where the judge’s spouse had divested her stock before the decision
issued, because the length of participation during the conflict and the substantive motions decided
in that period made the divestiture insufficiently curative. 106 F.4th 218. Centripetal and Shell Oil
are decisions of the Federal Circuit and Litovich is a decision of the Second Circuit. They are
persuasive authority, not binding Fourth Circuit law. Plaintiff does not read Litovich to hold that
every former holding creates continuing disqualification. He reads it to hold that divestiture after
substantive participation does not automatically eliminate the need for a remedy.

Harmlessness is addressed on the orders’ own terms. The discovery ruling in ECF No. 84
rests on a legal premise, that discovery cannot be authorized before a Scheduling Order, that the
District Judge can correct independently on the Rule 72(a) objections. The amendment ruling is
different. It rests on a case-specific finding of “ample opportunity” and on the selection of denial as
the consequence of nonproduction, with no determination of the pending requests for relief from
the deadline. ECF No. 84 at 2. A finding and a choice of consequence made by a judge whose
participation is questioned are not cured by a reviewing court’s confirmation that some
consequence was available. Plaintiff does not contend that review by the District Judge is legally
incapable of correcting either ruling. Plaintiff contends that the appropriate correction is
independent adjudication of the restored motions on their existing submissions, which the District
Judge can provide on the Rule 72(a) objections, and that vacatur removes the challenged rulings as
the baseline against which that adjudication would otherwise occur.

VI. ORDER-SPECIFIC APPLICATION AND PRESERVATION

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 14 PagelD# 965

ECF No. 84 should be vacated in full. It contains the denials of all three motions to be
restored, and no part of it operates independently of the challenged participation.

ECF No. 64 should be vacated as to the comparison requirement and the expired September
11 deadline. That requirement is the predicate ECF No. 84 enforced. Vacating the enforcement
while leaving the predicate in place would leave ECF No. 59 subject to the same condition and the
same consequence. ECF No. 64 is separately before the District Judge on the September
objections, which challenge it on grounds that do not depend on the financial evidence. ECF Nos.
66, 67, 68. If the evidence establishes disqualification as of October 7 but not as of September 9, the
independent challenge to ECF No. 64 remains pending on those grounds, and Plaintiff does not
represent that both orders were necessarily entered during the same proven conflict.

ECF Nos. 63, 65, and 82 are not targeted. Their hearing and certification provisions are not
prerequisites to the relief requested here, and Plaintiff’s objections to those provisions in ECF Nos.
66 and 67 remain pending. The acceptance of ECF Nos. 78 and 78-1 under ECF No. 82 is
preserved. ECF No. 62 is not targeted; ECF No. 26 remains withdrawn. The organizing principle is
procedural correction, not preservation of orders because they favored Plaintiff. Should the Court
consider broader vacatur necessary, Plaintiff requests that all authorized briefing be independently
preserved or re-accepted so that no party is required to resubmit it.

VII. TIMELINESS AND CONSIDERATION OF THE EVIDENCE

The financial ground was not included in the September objections or in the original
drafting of the Rule 72(a) objections because Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest.
Ballentine Decl. { 2. He presented the ground promptly after learning of it, in three coordinated
applications submitted the same day. The Fourth Circuit requires that a disqualification motion be
raised “at the earliest moment after knowledge of the facts,” and applies that requirement to §

455(b) as well as § 455(a). Kolon Indus. Inc. v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 748 F.3d 160, 169—

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 10 of 14 PagelD#
966

71 (4th Cir. 2014). The judge’s independent obligation under § 455(c) and the nonwaiver provision
of § 455(e) do not eliminate the litigant’s obligation; “waiver and timeliness are distinct issues.” Id.
Plaintiff does not argue otherwise. The showing here is that no interval of knowing delay exists.
Plaintiff requests express consideration of Exhibits A and B and the Declaration in deciding
this Motion, and, to the extent needed, in connection with the pending objections. The District
Judge’s authority to revise interlocutory orders on substantially different evidence, Carlson, 856
F.3d at 325, and the statute’s delegation of the remedy to the judiciary, Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 862,
each supply a basis for considering the evidence. The retrospective remedy should not depend
solely on whether the evidence is received within the ordinary scope of Rule 72(a) record review.

VII. RESTORATION, AFFIRMATIVE ADJUDICATION, AND INTERIM
PROTECTION

Restoration is not the endpoint requested. Vacatur supplies the procedural correction. Rules
15(a)(2), 15(d), and 26(d)(1) supply the separate bases for granting ECF Nos. 59, 15, and 54 on
their briefed merits, and the Rule 72(a) objections present those merits. Plaintiff requests that the
District Judge proceed, following vacatur, to grant those motions on the existing submissions, or
alternatively to direct their prompt independent determination.

The interim relief has four parts. First, suspension of further substantive action under the
challenged referral while the disqualification motion is determined and any administrative transfer
is effected. Second, suspension of further reliance on the nonproduction condition in ECF No. 64
while ECF Nos. 66 and 67, the Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84, and this Motion are
determined. Third, determination of the amendment and financial-conflict issues before, or
expressly within, any claim-terminating disposition of ECF Nos. 10, 21, or 45 that relies on the

exclusion of the proposed pleading. Fourth, express provision that the District Judge may grant

10

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document94_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 11 of 14 PagelD#
967

independently warranted relief on the Rule 72(a) objections without awaiting resolution of every
financial-conflict question.

A pause “calls for the exercise of judgment, which must weigh competing interests and
maintain an even balance,” and the applicant “must make out a clear case of hardship or inequity in
being required to go forward.” Landis v. N. Am. Co., 299 U.S. 248, 254-55 (1936). The burden
rests on the party seeking the pause. Williford v. Armstrong World Indus., Inc., 715 F.2d 124, 127
(4th Cir. 1983). Defendants have an interest in prompt disposition of their dismissal motions. The
hardship asserted is specific: claim-terminating adjudication on a pleading Plaintiff moved to
replace, under a condition imposed and enforced by a judge whose participation is questioned on
documentary evidence, while that question is pending before two judges of this Court. Defendants’
briefing is preserved in full. Each protection has a defined terminating event: determination of the
disqualification motion and completion of any transfer; determination of the identified objections
and this Motion; and entry of the order on the amendment and financial-conflict issues. Plaintiff
does not request a pause tied to the remaining hearing or certification disputes, and does not request

an indefinite stay.
